newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK GDP growth seen further above trend.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK GDP growth seen further above trend.

text.p: UK GDP data out on Friday are expected to show economic growth accelerated further above the trend rate in the first quarter of the year with the lively services industry still leading the way.

The Reuter consensus forecast suggests GDP grew 0.9 percent in the first quarter compared with 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter last year. This would push year-on-year growth up to 2.9 percent from 2.6 percent in the fourth quarter.

"The monthly indicators point to another strongish number. In particular, retail sales grew by 1.0 percent signalling continued buoyancy in the consumer sector," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"In line with that we expect services output to have expanded sharply again."

Service industry activity has driven the economic recovery over the last year or so. It recorded growth of 1.1 percent in the fourth quarter versus the third against manufacturing's 0.4 percent growth in the period.
Loynes forecasts service industry output growth still leads the way, but slowed slightly in the first quarter to 1.0 percent.
David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan, said manufacturing probably made a more significant contribution to overall GDP in the latest period than in the fourth quarter.
"Manufacturing has had a reasonable first quarter. January and February both saw a decent pick up versus the fourth quarter."
Official figures already released showed manufacturing output grew 0.6 percent in the three months to February versus 0.4 percent in the three months to January.
But Mackie said recent survey evidence showing export orders still very weak would mean continuing concern over the outlook for manufacturing.

The Confederation of British Industry said on Wednesday that export orders fell sharply in the four months to April, with firms' expectations for the next four months falling at the fastest rate for six years.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said the batch of data feeding into GDP breakdown has been inconclusive.

"Other guides to first-quarter activity are mixed. Employment continued to rise sharply but construction orders slipped slightly while private housing starts slowed, the level of hours worked fell slightly and utilities output fell."
Economists agreed if the GDP figures are in line with expectations, they will keep up pressure on the authorities to raise interest rates soon after the May 1 election.

And, if the polls are right, opposition Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown rather than current Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will meet Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George on May 7.
"Momentum is clearly building and growth is well above trend. I think Brown will have rates half a point higher by the end of June," said Mackie.
